Static vs dynamic codes for a short promotion

A static code has its destination — a link, a coupon code, a piece of text — baked into the pattern itself. It can never change, needs no account and no server: FreeQrly generates it entirely in your browser, with nothing uploaded and no tracking. A dynamic code holds a short redirect link instead. The printed pattern stays the same, but you can change where it points and see how many times it was scanned. Dynamic codes need a free sign-in to create.
For a three-day sale, that difference is the whole strategy — most shops need both, decided per placement, not per campaign.

The rule of thumb: if the offer is printed as text on the same poster ("20% off, code BF20"), the code can be static — the coupon text never changes. If the scan opens a web page whose content, price, or stock might change during the weekend, make it dynamic. The customer journey: see it, scan it, claim it, redeem it
A Black Friday QR code fails in exactly four places, one per step of the journey. Design for the step where shoppers actually drop off.

Figure 1: From poster to purchase. Four steps with arrows — see the code, scan it, claim the coupon, redeem it (in store at the till, or online at checkout). Note beneath: "Every step should take seconds. If a step needs typing, a login, or an app download, shoppers drop off."

See the code. The code has to be noticed before it can be scanned. Put it at eye level, give it a quiet margin of empty space, and add a short line saying what the scan gives: "Scan for 20% off" beats "Scan me", because it answers the passer's only question — what do I get?
Scan. It must work with the phone camera alone, no app — true of every code FreeQrly makes. Test on iPhone and Android before printing, in the real lighting, from the real distance.

Claim the coupon. The page the scan opens should show the discount and its terms on the first screen — percentage, minimum spend, expiry — with nothing to type and nothing to sign up for. Every extra field costs redemptions.

Redeem. In store, the customer shows the phone at the till. Online, the discount should already be applied at checkout, or the coupon should be one tap to copy. If redemption needs staff to look something up, or a customer to remember a string of characters, the journey breaks at the last step.

Printing and placement tips

Size follows distance. Rough rule: the code should be about one-tenth as wide as the distance it will be scanned from. A shelf tag scanned from 30 cm away can be 3 cm wide; a window poster scanned from the pavement needs at least 10 cm (4 in). When in doubt, print bigger.

Contrast is not optional. Dark code on a light background, always. A black code on a black poster, a gold code on yellow, or a code over a busy photo will not scan reliably in shop lighting. If the poster is dark, put the code on a white square.
Leave a quiet zone. Keep a clear margin around the code at least as wide as one of its small squares — no text, no logos, no border touching it.

Use high error correction for anything handled or outdoors. Set error correction to High or Max for receipts, flyers, and packaging that will be folded, rained on, or scuffed. Higher error correction lets the code survive damage; the trade-off is a slightly denser pattern.
Add your logo in the center, carefully. Keep it small — under about a fifth of the code's width — and use high error correction so the code still reads.
Print one, scan it, then print the rest. Print one copy of each design, scan it in the real location, from the real distance, in the real light, and only then print the batch.
Put the offer in words next to the code. "Scan for 20% off today only" tells a shopper why to bother. A bare code is decoration — and if a phone cannot scan it, the shopper can still read the offer.
Redemption and fraud: one-use vs unlimited coupons

Unlimited coupons are the default for a Black Friday doorbuster: one code, anyone can use it, no tracking of who redeemed. Simple, fast at a busy till, and right when the discount is modest and the goal is footfall. The risk is exactly what it sounds like — the code spreads. For a 10–20% storewide offer, that is usually acceptable; the sharing is the marketing.

One-use coupons make sense when the discount is deep — a high-value item, a big percentage, a free gift. One-use needs a system behind the code: a unique code per customer, a list the till can check, a way to mark it used. A single static code cannot do this — everyone scanning the same poster gets the same code. If you need one-use, generate unique codes per customer (Batch mode can make up to 50 at a time) and validate them at the till or at checkout.

Practical middle ground. Most small retailers do fine with unlimited codes plus three cheap controls: a clear expiry ("Friday only"), a minimum spend, and a per-transaction limit ("one discount per transaction"). Print them on the poster, show them on the landing page, enforce them at the till — no extra system needed.

Staff briefing matters more than software. Tell till staff in writing what each code does, its terms, and what to do when a customer shows a screenshot of someone else's phone. A five-minute Friday-morning briefing prevents more fraud — and more arguments — than any validation system.
After the sale, expire visibly. If a coupon has an expiry, honor it and say so on the poster. Nothing damages trust faster than a code that worked on Friday and silently fails on Saturday.

When the offer changes mid-sale

Repoint, don't reprint. This is the entire reason to use dynamic codes for sale pages and doorbusters. Edit the destination from your dashboard; the printed code keeps working. A reprint takes hours you do not have on a Friday.

Decide in advance what a sold-out code points to. The default should be the main sale page or the closest equivalent item — never a dead page, and never a page still advertising the sold-out item at the old price. Write the fallback in your code list during planning week.

Change the destination, then the poster text if you can. If the poster says "50% off headphones" and the headphones are gone, a small "sold out — see today's deals" sticker over the headline is honest and takes a minute. The code repoint does the rest.

Keep one person in charge of changes. Mid-sale edits by three people produce three different destinations. One person owns the dashboard for the weekend; everyone else routes requests through them. Log every change in one line — time, code, old and new destination.

Static or dynamic — which does a Black Friday sale need?

Both, for different jobs. Static for the coupon code itself: it carries the code as text and never expires. Dynamic for anything that changes — the sale page, hourly drops, stock that sells out. Dynamic codes are free with a sign-in, and the free tier includes 20 of them.
Can I change where a printed code points?

Yes — that is what dynamic means here. Edit the destination from your dashboard any time; the printed code never changes. Static codes cannot be changed after printing, which is why they suit fixed coupons only.
What happens to my codes after the sale?

Nothing expires. Repoint dynamic codes to your next campaign, and keep the posters for next year — same codes, new offers. Static codes keep working as long as the page or coupon behind them is still valid.
How big should a window poster code be?
Big enough to scan through glass from the sidewalk — 10 cm (4 in) or more. The rule is roughly one-tenth of the scanning distance, so test it from the pavement, not from inside the shop.
Can I make a different code for every product on sale?

Yes — use Batch mode in the generator: one link per line, or upload a CSV/XLSX file, up to 50 codes per batch, downloaded as a ZIP of PNGs. Batch is static-only, so use it for fixed per-product pages and coupons.
Do customers need an app to scan the code?
No. Every code opens with the phone's built-in camera. If a code seems to need an app, it was made wrong — test-scan with a plain camera before printing.
How do I stop a coupon from being shared all over social media?

You cannot stop a static coupon from being screenshotted. If the discount is deep, use one-use codes validated at the till instead of one shared code. For most storewide offers, an expiry date, a minimum spend, and a one-per-transaction limit are enough — and the sharing brings you customers.
